speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege and, under our rules, I take the first opportunity to do so and tell the Chair and all hon. members

May 8, 1978
Privilege-Mr. A. Lambert
how indignant I as well as my colleagues are with the CBC, as members of a registered Canadian political party whose national leadership convention took place in Winnipeg on May 7, 1978. In my opinion, that convention was a national event which deserved to be broadcast live, particularly by a Crown corporation which is supposed to promote harmony in Canada by reporting in an objective way the most significant national events either of a political, economic or social nature. Now, on May 6 and 7, a national leadership convention was held in Winnipeg to elect a new national leader of the Social Credit Party of Canada, the successor to Andre Fortin who was killed in an accident on June 24, 1977, after only seven months as leader and successor to Real Caouette, this great Canadian who has founded our party and directed it for 14 years.
Mr. Speaker, CBC was aware of this national political event since it had several reporters on the field who did their best considering they were not provided with the facilities for direct broadcasting of the main highlights of this convention. I do not blame the reporters but the management. I fail to understand why CBC, with a yearly budget of half a billion dollars out of the taxpayer's pocket, would not use part of this money to broadcast such an important political event, while it does not hesitate to allot broadcasting time to all kinds of sports programs. In this area, it goes to great lengths, but when the time comes to inform the public objectively on State affairs, it does not seem interested in promoting the commonweal as well as national harmony.
Mr. Speaker, the Social Credit Party of Canada is a national party whose activities deserve to be broadcast by the CBC at least as much as those of the Quebec Liberal party whose convention, last April, was extensively covered by the CBC. The Social Credit Party of Canada convention, which I attended together with many delegates from Quebec, took place in an orderly fashion, and we believe our activities are likely to promote harmony in Canada. I am convinced that our activities and the positions we took were not likely to urge the people to dissent and question the established order, to promote disorder, but were designed rather to explain to the people what options we have to offer as our contribution to the administration of our country.
Mr. Speaker, do we want or not to ensure the survival of our democratic system? If so, it is essential that all Canadians be given a fair deal in all areas, particularly with regard to information, especially from a Crown corporation like the CBC. What is happening exactly? For two weeks, we have seen on Parliament Hill several vans with CBC equipment and employees; I do not know for sure what they were doing there, but anyhow, it is a fact. I will not believe for a minute that it was not possible for the CBC to be in Winnipeg on May 7 with the required equipment to broadcast live at least the movers' and the candidates' speeches from 11 a.m. to noon, as well as part of the vote and the speech of the elected leader, as is done when the other Canadian parties hold their conventions.

Mr. Speaker, it is true that our party strongly opposes the financial dictatorship and the monopolistic handling of the nation's credit but that is no reason to treat us unfairly. Those are the kind of injustices which raise indignation among honest people who have the right to know the various options offered to them by the different Canadian political parties. The new leader of the Social Credit Party of Canada is the leader of a nationwide party and, as such, he is entitled to the same consideration as any other leader by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The economic, financial and political ideology which has inspired the administrative principles of provincial governments in Alberta for 35 years and in British Columbia for a quarter of a century deserved another kind of treatment, particularly when one considers that our political formation has had and still has members duly elected in the House of Commons, whether from the east or from the west.
Mr. Speaker, Canadian television viewers, either from the west or from the east, expected to have live coverage of the proceedings of that convention. They were deeply disappointed. The people of Quebec with more than 300 delegates attending the convention in an effort of co-operation toward greater harmony between eastern, central and western Canadians hoped to live those developments via the television. Air time is used for other things, offensive movies, cruel and violent movies, there is time for that! Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, and I draw your attention more particularly on that, on Saturday May 6 on the 10.30 news the words Progressive Conservative party were used to announce a convention of the Social Credit Party of Canada. Was that a mistake? If so, well, we have people who do not have much brains to carry out their responsibilities. If it was done on purpose, they should be fired. This is not the way to run democracy in this country.
Mr. Speaker, you will understand why as House leader of the Social Credit Party of Canada I am taking advantage of the first opportunity available to point that fact out to the whole people of this country so such situations will not be repeated, otherwise we are headed toward disorder. When they are treated injustly people end up revolting. Such injustices can turn pacific people into revolutionaries. Mr. Speaker, I want to conclude with a motion to show how logic we are in our comments and protests. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Abitibi (Mr. Laprise):
That this House force the management of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to appear before the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections to give before the said committee the reasons which prevented the corporation from broadcasting live the main events of the convention of the Social Credit Party of Canada which ended in Winnipeg on May 7, 1978.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for your kind attention.

speechtext:
that Bill C-39 be read the third time and do pass.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am happy to take part today in the debate on this bill which includes such interesting objectives as the creation of many jobs, the export of finished products which use our natural resources, the creation of an additional source of revenue for the federal government as well as for the provincial governments, an interesting, profitable and very promising breakthrough for a totally Canadian product on foreign markets, and last but not least, an excellent opportunity to enhance the international image of Canada through the work of our craftsmen and artists.
You are no doubt aware, Mr. Speaker, that the Royal Canadian Mint has succeeded for several years already in getting and maintaining the reputation of being one of the best mints in the whole world. Our special coins programs have always drawn very special attention on national and international numismatic markets. Within a few years, in hardly three years, we have succeeded in getting major deals for minting in Canada coins for more than 30 foreign countries.
Those successes, added to the great success of our coins programs in 1976 for the Olympics and last year to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the coronation of Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II, have allowed us to secure privileged position on the international numismatic market. Should we be proud of those successes? Yes, Mr. Speaker. Should we be satisfied with those successes? I do not think so, Mr. Speaker. New opportunities are available to us and we want to take advantage of them. That is in summary what is prompting us to introduce this legislation. Through this amendment which is really an administrative measure, we want to allow the Royal Canadian Mint to take greater advantage of the world numismatic market where last year we sold coins worth some $31 million. That is a very impressive performance. However, the overall annual coin market being evaluated at $1 billion, the government believes that the Royal Canadian Mint must continue to draw maximum benefit from it.
Currency and Exchange Act
We realize that a gold bullion coin program as presented to us by the representatives of the Canadian Mining Association appears to harbour a tremendous potential. Far from trying to dispute their claims, we have listened with an open mind. We have been impressed. We sense that for a number of reasons this market might be very ripe for Canada and, Mr. Speaker, we are prepared and ready to pursue actively with the Canadian Mining Association, the other interested industries, and in conjunction with the officials from the Department of Finance, the in-depth study of the potential of such a program and of its various implications for the Canadian government and for Canada as a whole. It would be less than responsible for me to recommend to cabinet a proposition that has not been thoroughly researched and which still contains a number of unanswered questions.
There are currency implications that need to be identified, clarified, and researched, in a more thorough manner than we have had time to do.
There are gold sourcing complications that so obviously require both short and long term planning far beyond what has been done up to this point. Although Canada happens to be the third largest gold producer in the world, our total output at present is approximately 1.5 million ounces of gold a year. This bullion coin program could absorb 2 million to 3 million ounces a year. Even if the prospects are very exciting, hon. members will agree with me that the question of the gold supply is one that will require a great deal of consultation, compromises, and commitments both from the gold mining industry and from the government as the holder of the Canadian gold reserves.
There are production and distribution set-ups that have to be put in place and that have to be guaranteed before the first coin ever reaches that market.
These are some of the questions that I and my officials have been asking ourselves concerning this program. But let me not leave hon. members with a feeling of pessimism about this program. That would be too easy a solution and one that Canada certainly does not need at this point in time. My comments should not be construed as being negative toward this new idea but rather of expressing my willingness to explore this innovative concept.
Let me assure hon. members that, although we have been asking questions, we know the answers will be forthcoming. We know that we have the people, the resources, and the desire to pursue this idea and to bring forth in due time recommendations to cabinet as to its feasibility and profitability.

If on the one hand we did not have time yet to explore thoroughly that new project, on the other hand we certainly have concrete evidence of the success obtained by our two previous gold coin programs. Our $100 gold coin program commemorating the Olympic Games, our first major initiative
5234

May 8, 1978
Currency and Exchange Act
in that field, sold nearly one million coins, which represents a total exceeding $100 million.
Last year, to mark the Jubilee of Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II, the Royal Canadian Mint issued another $100 gold coin. Over only four months, about 180,000 coins were sold for a total value of almost $25 million.
Those two programs were very successful owing to the numismatic quality of those coins and also to our strong marketing efforts. Now that this distribution system has been established and its efficiency proven, it deserves to be supported regularly to produce maximum benefits. Through this bill, the Royal Canadian Mint will be able to establish long term planning for that kind of numismatic coins which would certainly guarantee it an increasing share of that enormous international market and better profitability for its production facilities. This year we intend to issue once again a $100 gold coin. If one of the major assets of a numismatic coin is its technical quality, its artistic quality is also very important. There are excellent Canadian artists in this field and I wish to mention only one of them, Raymond Lee, a Toronto artist whose design of provincial floral emblems was chosen for the gold coin commemorating the Queen's Jubilee.
To facilitate the work of the artists and ensure a certain uniformity in their submissions it has been decided this year to select the theme of national unity. And the submissions already received seem particularly interesting. To conclude I wish to mention the excellent co-operation of several hon. members who have studied this bill in committee and particularly the work of my excellent parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson). Following their representations we made some amendments that will certainly facilitate its passage. First, the governor in council will be given this power for a period of three years only. The government will have to review that decision before January 1, 1981. Finally, the minister in charge commits himself to report to Parliament every six months on the relevant details of this gold coin program. Far from infringing on the rights of Parliament, this bill will enable hon. members to follow very closely the progress made, and to judge over the next few years the benefits derived from such a program.

speechtext:
In answer to the first part of the question, the theme for the current year was the choice of the board of directors of the Royal Canadian Mint. It was not imposed by the government. In fact, the reverse is the case. Now that the board of directors has decided on a theme, the ratification of the governor general in council needs to be obtained, so whether it is advisable to use this particular theme in the present year has still to be considered. I am ready to take into account arguments directed to this question. Indeed, the expression of such opinions will help the cabinet make a final decision.
With regard to the later part of the question, if we are given authority within the next four hours to proceed with the gold coin program, the first pieces will normally be issued next fall-I cannot give a specific date. That is what I am told. The urgency is this: we do not wish to lose the momentum of what we now consider to be an established world market for Canadian coins of this type. Every year, now, collectors will expect Canada to issue such a coin and, if we are not in a position to do so, the marketing of this national resource in the form of a finished product would suffer an important disruption.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO AUTHORIZE ISSUANCE OF CERTAIN GOLD COINS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the first to take part in this debate on behalf of the official opposition I should like to say at the outset that we have some rather grave reservations with respect to the bill now before us.
We expressed those reservations during the committee stage and were able to secure two significant amendments to the bill as presented. First, the authority we could be giving to the

May 8, 1978

cabinet with respect to the minting of gold coinage would be operative only between the present date and January 1, 1981. In the second place, there would be a provision for reporting at six-month intervals back to parliament setting out exactly what had been done in terms of the coinage which had been minted.
These amendments have made the bill somewhat more acceptable, but there is a fundamental misunderstanding with respect to what we are now considering. The mining industry in Canada is interested, almost eager, to see the Mint put out what is generally referred to as a bullion gold coin. The most popular form of such a coin is, of course, the South Africa Krueger Rand, a 1-ounce gold coin priced directly in relation to the current value of gold. If, for example, the price of gold is $160 an ounce, the price of the Krueger Rand coin would be $160, give or take whatever is needed for the commission. This is what the mining industry is hoping will be minted in Canada.
However, I sense that what the government is mainly interested in is not the production of a gold bullion coin but another commemorative coin. And, of all things, what it is thinking of, to judge what was said by the minister, is a gold coin commemorating national unity! Such a coin, to be widely distributed throughout the world, would, by its very terminology be broadcasting to all the other nations, in effect, that there is some kind of disunity question. This is a strange twist. The domestic problem suddenly becomes glossed over by the minting of a gold coin on the theme of national unity, a coin which will be circulated around the world, broadcasting the message that somehow or other disunity in Canada is something which must be considered.
I do not know who are the public relations officers for the government or for the Mint. The minister told us it was the board of directors of the Mint who decided on this theme. In my opinion a new set of public relations officers is needed.
It is utter rubbish to suggest that a country as great as Canada, which has experienced 110 years of Confederation, can find no theme to put on a coin other than that of national unity. Let us take a more positive theme, for example, a theme commemorating our great scientists, or, if you like, our great statesmen, or our great northern frontier. Let us choose a theme based on the positive things we have to be proud of, and let us not become consumed with the issue of national unity when it comes to an application of this kind.
We have misgivings about what the government is trying to do, on three grounds. First, we believe the government should be more candid on the subject of the issuance of a gold bullion coin. If the minister has no interest in issuing such coins, let him say so, and let those concerned judge the government accordingly. In any case, he should quit pussyfooting around- today, for instance, the minister indicated that an in-depth study would be conducted. Our second reservation has to do with the theme of these commemorative coins which are to be brought forward in the fall. Our third and more fundamental concern has to do with the way in which the government is treating the coinage of this country.
Currency and Exchange Act
Hon. members will recall that the government got into a very odd deal at the time of the Olympics. In order to get the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) off the hook with regard to his promise that he would never use taxpayers' money to fund the Olympics, the government came up with the odd concept of minting Olympic coins. They were legal tender, but as far as their seigniorage was concerned the proceeds were to go to the Olympic Corporation as opposed to the treasury of Canada. At various stages of that legislation we in the official opposition opposed it because we felt the government was being reckless with the coin of the realm and that greater safeguards should have been included. In fact, to some extent at our urging safeguards were put into the legislation to ensure that the coinage would not be completely debased or used in a way which traditionally coinage of this country is never used, that is, for private gain of some concern outside the government or the people of Canada. There was a rather sad spectacle with regard to the Olympic coinage.
The Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) said today that the government has had great success with its coin programs and that he was hoping that this would continue. That is just balderdash. There has not been success with coinage programs. Let me give the House some figures. For those who are interested I am referring to the report to parliament as of September 30, 1977, of the Minister of Finance with respect to the Olympic coins. As we all know, the Minister of Finance was required to report to parliament regarding various aspects of that program.
As of September 30 the face value of Olympic coins issued pursuant to the Olympic (1976) Act was $279,692,765. Olympic coinage of a face value of almost $280 million was sold. Here is the real grabber. Guess how much of that money ended up with the Olympic Corporation? How much of the almost $280 million actually found its way to the Olympic Corporation? At the bottom of page nine of the report of the Minister of Finance it shows that the aggregate amount of all payments to the Olympic Corporation was $100 million. By the time sales costs, which were astronomical, and other costs-the various minting costs and so forth-were written off-almost $180 million had dribbled away, and only $100 million went to the Olympic Corporation.
Our coinage was debased. We put a few grains of silver into coins and called them silver coins. We then put a few grains of gold into some other coins and called them gold coins. We sold them around the world saying that they were silver and gold coins, but the fact is that they were neither. In each case there was only a percentage of silver or gold. There has to be a stop to this debasing of the nation's currency.
The inflation we have in this country is due largely to the unfortunate printing of money which has been carried out by this government through its control of the Bank of Canada. I am not saying that we should return to the gold standard, that somehow gold should become a new standard or barometer or that we should not issue a gold coin which is not 100 per cent gold, but I think it is questionable as to how long Canada
5236

May 8, 1978
Currency and Exchange Act
should be in this game of minting coins, not because we need them for general commerce or for trade, but because the government thinks this is a cute little gimmick it can use to sell coins to people around the world who are coin collectors. That is what is before us today. How long should we tolerate gimmicks with regard to our coinage?
The coin which is contemplated to be sold under the theme of national unity will not be 100 per cent gold. It will have some portion of gold. We will hear later how much gold will be in it. It will sell for something over $100. It will have a face value of $100, but the truth is that, just like the Franklin mint or any other private minting operation, the government more and more is getting into the game of creating coinage, not because it is needed for commerce, which is the basic reason we have coinage and paper money, but because it is a cute gimmick to make a few dollars on the side and because there are many people who are willing to buy these coins. This is Barnum and Bailey stuff. If Barnum and Bailey had had the authority, they certainly would have been involved in this in order to get a few more shekels into their coffers.
The sad thing is that this illustrates as much as anything how this government is not inclined to deal with the fundamental problems we have, but is going for tokenism and for these symbolic things, and thinking it is solving problems by bringing out a $100 gold coin and calling it a national unity coin. What would have had a more positive effect would have been a government which showed proper restraint in its spending and which demonstrated to Canadians and to other investors throughout the world that it did have meaningful plans to reduce the deficit with which we are living.
The tokenism has to end. The idea of creating coinage with a theme which will be beneficial as far as national unity is concerned misses the point. There are basic problems which must be solved. Let the government get on with solving them, and the national unity problem it speaks of will solve itself. We need something more fundamental than the minting of another coin.
The inflation we have in Canada is due in large measure to the overprinting of money in relation to our real growth. Let there be no doubt that the inflation we have is due, to a large extent, to the overprinting of money. From 1973 to the end of 1977 our average inflation rate has been 9.3 per cent. If we were to project that ahead until 1981, the purchasing power of the 1977 dollar would be 70 cents, and the purchasing power of the 1971 dollar would be only 44 cents. Since the emperor took power in Canada our dollar has fallen below 50 cents in value compared with what it was valued at in purchasing terms the year the emperor took over. With that type of inflation and with that type of devaluation in terms of purchasing power, this government now comes before us and tells us that one of the top priorities of the government is to get parliament to pass Bill C-39 permitting the government to mint a debased gold coin. That is nothing short of shocking.
Let me give the House some other figures. If the government allows 9.3 per cent inflation to continue-and we cer-

tainly have no evidence that it will try to restrain its spending-every eight years we will double the level of inflation.
Not only have we inflation, but now we have the result of virtually uncontrolled inflation, which is rising unemployment. Here again, if we are to project ahead and if this government, heaven forbid, should ever be allowed to continue in power, we will have, by 1981, 1,280,000 Canadians out of work. That figure is compiled by simply following the trend that has developed since 1973 as a result of the economic activities of this government.
These are hard figures. For example, real growth has fallen in the last four years to slightly over 3 per cent. In fact, if it is projected ahead to 1981, we will find that we will be five years behind so far as our target of social growth is concerned. Those are the facts, and here we have the government of the day saying that there is nothing more serious in Canada than the authority, which it wants, to mint a $100 gold coin in the name of national unity. There are over one million Canadians out of work; inflation in Canada is running at 9.3 per cent; real growth, if it is projected ahead to 1981, is five years behind; and the government of the day is saying that the most urgent thing for Canadians is to mint a new gold coin commemorating national unity.
Let me mention something else, and this is perhaps the saddest spectacle of all. Let us take a look at the deterioration of revenue in this country so far as the federal budgetary position is concerned compared with federal budgetary expenditures. In 1975 revenue went up about 28 per cent at the federal level. In that year the government's expenditure went up 28 per cent. In other words, the government spent 28 per cent more in 1975 than in 1974 and that was, luckily for members of the government, the amount of revenue they had that year.
I mentioned that year because let us not forget that was the year the government spent money to be re-elected. The 28 per cent spending spree which we saw in the fiscal year 1975 started in 1973 and was amplified in 1974. The name of the game was to get re-elected at any cost, come what may. If inflation in the country were to go up, Mr. Turner, who was the minister of finance, under the dictates of the emperor of the day, the Prime Minister, obviously said, "Let her go". That is what we in Canada are now living with. We are living with the aftermath of what the government did to secure its re-election in 1974, because it was so disturbed by being put in a minority position on October 30, 1972, that it said, "Turn up the printing presses, get federal government spending in motion, give the people an illusion of wealth, and let the inflationary consequences come later". Ministers thought they could ride out the inflationary consequences as well as the unemployment which would result.
Here are the figures. They said they were on a restraint kick. The fact is that in 1976 expenditures in this country went up by 16 per cent; in 1977 they went up 14 per cent; and in 1978 they went up 10 per cent. The average rate of increase in
May 8, 1978

expenditures since 1974, the last year that we had an election in this country, has been 17 per cent. For the government of the day, with that kind of background, with a 17 per cent increase in fiscal spending, to be coming to parliament on May 8 saying; "Give speedy passage to the currency exchange Bill C-39 so that we can mint a few more gold coins on the national unity theme" shows the priority that this government has and how little concern it has for the level of inflation which exists now in the country, and for the unemployment levels.
Having said that, I would like to state, if I may, why I feel it is unfortunate that the government has developed the attitude it has with regard to gold. Gold is a unique commodity, whether we like it or not, and has been in that unique position for centuries. In any civilized country you will find that gold has played a unique role for centuries.
Various books have been written on the subject of gold. One which I read over the Easter break was entitled "The Golden Constant-The English and American Experience, 15601976". It was written by Roy W. Jastram, Professor of Business Administration at the University of California, Berkeley. In this book, which is a compilation of various data concerning prices, the price of gold and the relationship of prices to gold, the author reaches some very interesting conclusions. If I may, I should like to read parts of the book into the record. At page 179 of this book, Mr. Jastram says:
Gold prices do not chase after commodities; commodity prices return to the index level of gold over and over. This is one of the principal findings of my study.
Let me explain. It is commonly said-and certainly the author of this book has mentioned-that gold is thought to be a good hedge against inflation. The author points out that, if you look at the last 400 years, that assumption is not correct. Gold is not necessarily a good hedge against inflation. But he does point out that it is a tremendous hedge in times of a depression because, as a rule, if you have held gold during depression periods, you have made your best money.
What the author is saying in what I have just quoted is that there seems to be an odd relationship between commodity prices and gold, and that commodity prices can get out of line but eventually they return to the constant price of gold. He gives decade by decade, and in fact century by century, proof of what he is saying. To quote him again from page 179 of his book, he writes;
My feeling is that it is beyond rational belief that this event could occur by chance alone, with the observed frequency, over the last three centuries.
He points out that this is why gold is constant. He then goes on to point out that there are various forms that a gold standard can take if a nation wishes to go on the gold standard. He says:
The essential characteristics of the classical gold-coin standard are as follows:
All forms of money, paper and otherwise, are held at a parity with a coined monetary unit defined by its gold content and are convertible into this gold coin on demand.
This monetary unit is coined freely, without an appreciable charge for the process itself.
Gold coins circulate freely and may be freely exported, imported, or melted down.
Currency and Exchange Act
Gold is unlimited legal tender.
Gold constitutes a large part of the nation's central monetary reserve.
The author then goes on to state that, with some risk of oversimplification, it can be said that governments of the day tend to change this type of gold standard in various ways, which he enumerates as follows:
1.	Paper currency does not have a 100 per cent gold reserve behind it. There is not enough bullion in the world today to support world-wide trade, commerce, and finance on a one-to-one basis of paper to gold ...
2.	The world price of gold may increase (drastically, as it has in the 1970s) so that either the admissible volume of paper currency will automatically inflate or the required reserve ratio of gold will have to be reduced correspondingly.
3.	If the price of gold is to be held constant by the marketplace, gold must be bought or sold by the government in quantities precisely decided by the government, or interest rates adjusted by central banks to accomplish the same purpose by indirection.
4.	If the price of gold is to be held constant by edict, the market for gold must be interdicted by the government, for example, exports forbidden, imports embargoed, private boardings outlawed, and so on.
Governmental interference at any one of these points is, of course, a denial of laissez faire. This is not to say that a gold standard would be impossible today. It is to say that the gold standard as a dehumanized, self-disciplining dispenser of monetary justice is a myth.
Any monetary system needs to be managed. The real questions are how and to what extent.
What are the basics people understand when it is said that we should follow the gold standard? To what degree is it realistic to expect any nation to go on a gold standard today? As the author indicated, it is not realistic to expect nations to return to any type of gold standard.
Why is there concern about gold? There is concern about gold because it has remained a rather constant thing through the centuries. If our citizens wish to have a convenient way to hold gold, they should be allowed to do that. That is why we support the concept of a $100 or $50 gold bullion coin. It provides Canadians with a convenient way to acquire gold coins. It saves them from buying the most popular bullion coin, the Kruger Rand. It provides them with a convenient way to hold gold, which has been done traditionally by people over the centuries. It is not that those people will be able to keep up with inflation by holding gold, but it will provide them with a constant which they can hold, along with their other investments, in order to ensure, if economic problems occur, that constant will retain its buying power, whereas various other investments will not hold the same buying power.
Page 189 of the same book in part reads as follows:
Gold has two interesting properties: it is cherished and it is indestructible. It is never cast away and it never diminishes, except by outright loss. It can be melted down, but it never changes its chemistry or weight in the process ...
Its price has been remarkably similar for centuries at a time. Its purchasing power in the middle of the twentieth century was nearly the same as in the midst of the seventeenth century.
As far as I am concerned, that is a significant thing. Gold has remained relatively constant in its purchasing power over the centuries. It is unfortunate that our government has taken the concept of minting gold coins and debased it in the name of making money. There is nothing wrong with bringing out a

May 8, 1978
Currency and Exchange Act
gold coin in Canada. In fact a S20 gold coin was brought out at one point. That coin contained $20 worth of gold. Now it sells at a substantial premium of well over $100 because the gold contained in that coin has a purchasing power today which is comparable to what it was then.
If the government is given the authority to mint the commemorative coins it talks about, a fraud will be perpetuated on the buyers of those coins. This coin is referred to as a $100 gold coin. Many people will buy it thinking that it contains $100 worth of gold, without realizing that it contains very much less gold. In short, they are paying for something at a premium which does not contain $100 worth of gold. It is a shame to use our currency in that manner. It is a shame that money cannot be made internationally in a more effective manner than simply taking the coin of the realm, striking new themes, and attempting to flog it around the world in order to make whatever revenue the government sees fit. With the billions of dollars of imbalance in Canada, surely there is a more meaningful way to bring revenues into the coffers of our country without debasing the coinage of our land.
We have grave doubts about parliament's wisdom in providing the cabinet with authority to go ahead with any minting program concerning gold coins. Those doubts have been lessened somewhat by the 30-month limitation on the authority and the six-month reporting under the Olympic Coinage Act. It is time for the government to come to its senses. It should realize that many of the things it has done over the past decade obviously are not working. One cannot count on building a credit economy indefinitely, without the resultant repercussions of inflation and unemployment such as we are experiencing today.
If I had more time, I would speak-

If I were to talk until parliament is dissolved, knowing how upset the emperor is with the polls today, perhaps I would talk well into 1979.
In conclusion, I should like to direct the attention of hon. members to a book entitled, The Coming Credit Collapse. It is an interesting book which deals with world economy and currencies. It is authored by Mr. Alexander P. Paris, who is well known in the economic world. His degrees include a B.A. and an M.B.A. from Michigan State, and an M.A. in economics from Wayne State. He has been an active executive with various international trading organizations. In his book Mr. Paris pointed out that the credit explosion which has occurred cannot continue, and it will collapse if there is not more restraint and responsibility at the governmental level. In view of that, we should be very careful when we deal with the bill

before the House now. It is another small step toward further irresponsibility in the handling of Canadian economic affairs.
How much trust can we have in the government of the day? Because of the current account deficit, the government went into international markets to borrow funds, and it is not even aware of who its creditors are at the present time. I was not present in the Chamber on Friday, but I read Hansard of that date. I could hardly believe what I read when I discovered the Prime Minister thought he had borrowed $3 billion on behalf of the Canadian public from Citibank in New York. How totally out of touch can the Prime Minister be, and presumably the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien)? They went to bed on Thursday night believing that the $3 billion credit was arranged with Citibank in New York. Yet the Prime Minister indicated that if Citibank took in deposits from somebody in South Africa, so what, that was their business. I invite Your Honour to telephone New York and find out the facts. Citibank did not put up more than $175 million of that $3 billion credit. They could not because they are restricted to the amount they can put out on any one credit and they in turn syndicated the loan around the world.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO AUTHORIZE ISSUANCE OF CERTAIN GOLD COINS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not know how much more directly I can deal with the bill. The bill is the new Currency and Exchange Act, and the specific power that the government is asking for is the right to mint various gold coins. These gold coins become part of our over-all money supply, and what I am saying is that that money supply has been over-inflated and extended through the unwise use of credit in this country beyond all limits. I am simply saying that, considering the past decade, how much trust we have in the government of the day which, come 1978, is forced to borrow on international markets, and the Prime Minister does not even know who his creditors are with respect to the borrowings that they have had to arrange in New York to shore up our dollar?
It is all one ball of wax, and all I am saying is that I would have expected, at least days after the event, that the Prime Minister and his Minister of Finance would have realized that the loan or line of credit they received was one that was actually syndicated around the world, and that a portion of that standy-by credit was offered to South African banks as it was offered to various other banks including Arab banks and so on. I find it rather shocking that they are so little in touch with what in reality is happening that they did not know that simple fact.
I know that hon. members wish to speak further on this bill.
I hope that it will not be passed simply as an administrative function because it is much more serious than that. In short, I think it is another example of a rather irresponsible attitude on the part of this government with respect to a very, very serious
May 8, 1978

matter in this country, and that is the unsatisfactory economic condition of the nation.
Perhaps I did not have to speak so long, but surely if anybody had watched "The Nation's Business" on Sunday night they would have seen the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) trying to defend the economic record of this government, and they would have drawn only one conclusion, and that would be it is a dismal record.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO AUTHORIZE ISSUANCE OF CERTAIN GOLD COINS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking on third reading, I would like to say first that I come from an area where much of the economy has been built on the gold mining industry. In my opinion, we have done a great deal for the rest of Canada and its development, through the gold mining industry. It was with deep regret that we saw the passing of gold mines in Kirkland Lake, Larder Lake, Timmins and Matachewan, Pickel Crow, and other little communities across northern Ontario, and the fact that not much could be done to help them.
Over the years I have followed with great interest this argument that the member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) raised in relation to gold. I take very seriously his comment, which was facetious I know, when he said that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) did not really know where he was borrowing the money from and thought he was borrowing it from someone, but it turns out he is borrowing it from somebody else altogether, with a very small portion of it actually coming from Citibank. That highlights the inability of this government and of preceding governments, both Conservative and Liberal, to get through the morass of financial arrangements that exist around the myth, and I think it is a myth, of gold, the gold standard, the silver standard, and other backings we have for money.
The only things you can back money with are resources and work. Those are really the only two things that back any economy, and you can use whatever yardstick you want. We got along fine in this country without either gold or money for a long time, when we used beaver pelts. You piled them up so high against a rifle and that was the number of pelts you paid to purchase that rifle. When we talked about gold 20 years ago we were only talking about a yardstick. The yardstick got too expensive and was artificially controlled at a very low price. We controlled it throughout the world at $35 for years, after going up from $28. Now the actual price is $42.50, but in practice it does not amount to that at all.
In 1976 the mining industry came to the minister of mines in Ottawa and asked him for some help because the price of gold rose up to $150 and dropped back to a little over $100. When he was asked for help he made the statement that "he could not subsidize the gold industry to protect the miners and the mining communities because, if he did, he would have to subsidize other industries as well." Well, we have subsidized those other industries. It would be very interesting to know how much money we have paid to keep the rubber goods industry in this country, and how much we have subsidized the textile industry. However, we have not been able to do too much to save either one of them in the process. We could not
Currency and Exchange Act
do anything to help the gold mining industry for the very simple reason that we were in love with the International Monetary Fund.
The International Monetary Fund was born out of the failure of the Bretton Woods Agreement, when the Bretton Woods Agreement decided that one of the major factors in the last depression, which really resulted in World War II, was the inability of governments to provide enough money to make the purchases that were necessary. There was an unequal balance between the cost of goods, the necessity of those goods, and the dollars that were looking for those goods. It was decided that we would not curtail our money supply but that we would operate it on the basis suggested under the Bretton Woods Agreement where we would, in effect, maintain gold at $35 but "demonetize" the gold to the point where it was no longer the official backing of the money that was being put out.
They went further in the International Monetary Fund to where they allowed the world to establish drawing rights, and those drawing rights did not have to be backed with gold. That has failed because, while the countries and the banks put up a large amount of money for the International Monetary Fund to assist in the very worth-while project of developing the third world countries, almost none of those third world projects have repaid the money. There are billions of dollars, approximately $500 billion, floating around the world. Approximately $300 billion American are floating in Europe, and if those dollars were called, the United States would be bankrupt tomorrow. For this reason the President of the United States withdrew the backing of gold on dollars so that you can no longer redeem a dollar with gold backing. This has resulted in $300 billion floating around in Europe that are not worth the paper on which they are written. They are only worth that amount if they will be accepted by somebody else in trade, and everyone is very nervous about that. For this reason there is much collection of gold by private individuals.
There has been a lot of manipulation in gold by governments. The reason the mining industry was hurt in 1976 was not because of anything they did. They had raised wages in the industry over the years and had done some other things which brought them into the twentieth century. When I worked in that industry we often accused them of being in the nineteenth century because of their attitude toward workers and working conditions, but eventually they brought wages and conditions into line. That brought their cost up to $130, but they maintained that theirs was only a temporary problem and that gold would go to $200. They asked the government for help, but were refused. That was shortsighted of the government, Mr. Speaker. There are about 22 million ounces of gold in the treasury which were accumulated between 1948 and 1974 when we operated under what was called the Emergency Gold Mines Assistance Program. We accumulated about $1 billion worth of gold at $35 per ounce plus the maximum assistance of $10.27. If we are still holding that gold which was accumulated at about $47 per ounce and which is now worth $200 per

May 8, 1978
Currency and Exchange Act
ounce on the market-in fact we could sell it to the United States for more than $200 per ounce-we are in good shape.
We helped the mining communities for 15 years and made a lot of money. We only did badly when we took the advice of the Department of Finance to send it to Fort Knox in the United States at $35 per ounce. We lost $10.27, the EGMA subsidy, in that way but made a lot of money on the gold we have-in fact something in excess of $150 on today's market.
For these reasons I was interested in the gold coin proposition. It was an indication that the government was on the right track-not the officials of the Department of Finance, because they are plain stupid. There are 2,000 economists working for the government, who earn in excess of $30,000 per year. I think every one of them went to the same school and learned the same thing, but since they left the universities they have not learned anything. They really are not very bright.
The government decided to issue a gold coin, for two reasons: first, it is a good way to commemorate certain events and, second, there is a big market in the numismatic field. The government was already selling silver dollars. At one time it sold one of each coin in a celophane package, worth about $1.91 for $3. The mint did quite well on that. Now they package them in boxes and, for a coin worth $20, you pay $40, but it can sell for $200 on the market. I would not be surprised if the Department of Finance, being a bunch of pack-rats, put the lot in a backroom somewhere and eventually they will really be worth something. I know that in my office I put them in a drawer in a cabinet, and eventually they disappeared by attrition. Perhaps that also happens in the Department of Finance, but eventually they will reach the market and make some money, we hope.
I am in favour of the coin business, Mr. Speaker, and I think we have done a good job. I am quite proud of the Mint. In fact I am quite proud of the Post Office because our artists produce some excellent designs and they are well executed. Proof coins in this country are as good as any I have seen anywhere. I did not see anything wrong with the first $20 coin we issued, although ministers of finance made a lot of fuss. When the Hon. Donald Fleming was minister of finance we had not seen gold coins in Canada for 20 years. He got some bad advice from his departmental officials who told him we would be back on the gold standard and be the laughing stock of the world if we issued a gold coin. As a result he decided not to issue one. The next minister was the late George Nowlan, who got the same bad advice and did not issue a coin either. When Walter Gordon became minister of finance he was persuaded it would be a good idea to issue a gold coin for the centennial. That turned out to be successful, and a number of gold coins have been produced since.
It is interesting now to see how the Department of Finance officials are all in favour of this program and even suggest that the Mint can run a night shift. If we are going to issue something in the order of 190,000 of these coins with a half ounce or less of gold in each, that will not use much of the 22 million ounces of gold that we have. If we were going to go to the bullion coin, that is, a coin issued by the country which has

to be coinage and has to be legal tender, I would suggest that it be low in face value, say a $50 coin. The government is going to be broke and the mines are going to be broke. We will be looking at a new economic ball game because, if the price of gold falls to $50 per ounce, so will everything else fall. I hope I have lived out my days by the time these gold coins turn up in the banks at $50 each. The $50 will not be the redeemable amount but it will be legal tender.
That one ounce of gold will be in competition with the Krueger Rand and the Swiss and French gold coins-

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO AUTHORIZE ISSUANCE OF CERTAIN GOLD COINS
speechtext: And popcorn souvenirs.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO AUTHORIZE ISSUANCE OF CERTAIN GOLD COINS
speechtext:
The hon. member mentioned popcorn souvenirs. Right now they are selling for something like $176 so, if that is a popcorn souvenir, that is fine because a lot of people are buying them. In October, 1977, South Africa sold 405,000 Krueger Rands versus 216,000 in the year before that. As I understand it, South Africa is only issuing one coin, the one-ounce gold Krueger Rand which is not legal tender. The price is set by their government and is subject to change. South Africa is by far the world's largest producer of gold and we are told that they use between 10 and 15 per cent in this form. There is a fast growing international market for the coin.
A representative of the mining industry told us in committee that we are producing about 1.6 million ounces a year. There were 110 producing mines and today there are only ten or 12 left. Two or three of those mines are threatening to close within the next few years unless incentives are provided for development of new ore properties to make them worth-while.
I was impressed by the minister indicating that he really had not been advised up to that date of the potential. The minister's role is not really to sell gold. That job belongs to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie). He said there is no way he would have anything to do with that. So I was not surprised that the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) was not too familiar with this matter. I think he was pleasantly surprised to learn that the mining industry anticipates that sales in the first year could consume two million ounces of newly minted gold. If that is so, it would mean that we would have to increase our production to close to the three million ounces a year to meet the new demand and continue with the contracts the mining industry already has in the industrial field. It does mean an increase in mining, and that would only be the beginning.
There are not many people in Canada, unless they are in the finance department, who would not agree that gold being produced in Canada and sold as a coin, backed by the Canadian government to a degree by indicating its fineness, its karat and other characteristics as well as a limited legal tender, would not have a better appeal than South African gold on the world market. How many people in the United States buying gold in large quantities are buying Krueger Rand because there is no alternative? I believe these people would buy
May 8, 1978

Canadian coins if there were no difference in price or in any other way simply because they are not satisfied with the political regime in South Africa. I believe it would soon evolve into a voluntary boycott by all sales agents in the United States and, instead of handling South African coinage, they would handle Canadian coinage as a replacement. If that were the case we would have to be prepared to go into production on a large scale in the first year. The Master of the Mint has said there would be no difficulty in his field in going into production to that degree very quickly. As well, he has expressed the view that the Mint could go into production within a very short time.
I believe the minister was enthusiastic in this regard. As I said he does not hold the mining portfolio or the financial portfolio. I am sure that he saw an opportunity for one of the agencies under his control, the Canadian Mint, to expand its operation, employ more people, and maybe make a profit as well. There was no indication that we would do this for nothing. It would carry a cost that would cover the production costs of the Mint and carry the cost of the Department of Finance for picking up the gold and having it for a short period of time. There was no indication that this would be a cost. However, I believe he will run into all those red necks, or whatever you call them, who are terrified there will be an implication that we will hurt in any way, shape or form, the International Monetary Fund and that we will establish the gold standard in Canada again.
It seems to me that Canada is lucky because there is a large amount of gold available in this country. There are and have been mining prospects in every province of the nation, with the exception of Prince Edward Island. These prospects add a price. The price of gold depends entirely upon the amount of reserves there are available. The higher the price goes, the larger the reserves are; the lower the price, the less reserves there are. By doubling the price of gold it is probable that the lifetime of some of those mines that are to close within the next two or three years will be extended by 20 times. What yesterday was waste will be valuable ore tomorrow.
On behalf of the gold mining industry I sincerely hope that the minister will be able to persuade some of the other cabinet ministers that what we are talking about is not going back on to the gold standard and not going back into monetized gold in the true sense, but going into business to take gold, prefabricate it into a coin, and to put it on the market for those who wish to buy it as a commodity.
It is interesting to note that holdings are not that large. In 1970 767 tons were being prefabricated in the world. In 1976 that figure went up to 823 tons. In 1976 total fabrication was 1,359 metric tons of gold. For medallions, fake coins and official coins there were 178 metric tons. For private bullion, which category these coins fit into, there were 89 metric tons going into that field.
Our gold production last year was only 52.4 metric tons. The bullion market was 89 million tons. For Canada to get involved in that to the degree anticipated, we would be talking
Currency and Exchange Act
about several hundred metric tons. That would mean a great increase in the production of gold across Canada.
I do not see that this proposal will upset, influence, or shake money markets. If there is any way that could be done, it is already in effect. Money markets are being shaken all over the world. Revaluation and devaluation are rapidly taking place. In my opinion, very shortly in some countries around the world there will be a devaluation and deflation will take place. That will create a large market for this type of bullion coin which will be used as a hedge.
I support the idea of this matter coming back to parliament by regular report. I appreciate the minister making that decision in committee. He said he would do it without consulting anybody, which is a good sign. He also made the suggestion, without consulting anybody, that he would be prepared to pursue this idea of bullion coins. I hope he will have great success. This is the first bright light that has shone on the gold mining industry since the price of gold started fluctuating so rapidly two or three years ago. It does not mean that the gold mining industry will make more money. What it does mean is that the amount used in fabrication each year will be stabilized.
These gold bullion coins will provide a stabilizing factor in our mines. They are not asking for a hand out. However, the relationship between the Canadian dollar and the United States, Europe, and other parts of the world, means that this industry is more the victim of our economic structure than any other segment of our economy. They will certainly be more than appreciative if the government brings about some stability, even if that is through the minting of gold coins.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I entered the debate on second reading some days ago. At that time I was pleased to give approval to the bill for second reading in order to get it into committee where we could properly examine what was going on. That, of course, happened. It had three days in committee where, I am sorry to say, we did not get the kind of answers that the government should have provided to the opposition parties.
The overwhelming complaint that was raised at second reading of this bill was the fact that these coins would be produced by the authority of an order in council. In other words, it was the government's intention to take away the power of parliament in one fell swoop for all time with regard to gold coins. That point was raised over and over again, in particular by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). That avenue was explored in the committee. It is my opinion that the government and the minister did not come up with the proper answers to that complaint.
It was said at one of the committee hearings that it would not be possible for the Mint to plan ahead sufficiently without a bill like this in order to lay out the possibilities for production and planning in the Mint. I wish to refer to the minutes of the April 27 meeting of the Standing Committee on Finance,
5242

May 8, 1978

Trade and Economic Affairs, issue No. 24.1 asked the Master of the Mint the following question:
Would it be possible to operate the coin scheme that the Mint wants to operate under the guidance of a bill which was more specific than this?
The Master of the Mint replied:
It would surely be possible, Mr. Clarke, because in the past I think the approvals of gold coins have been specific approvals. The problem with a specific approval is you have approval for one program but the market for gold coins is a very important one abroad.
He went on to explain the marketing of gold coins. I may touch on that later. At that meeting the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services (Miss Nicholson) was only able to refer to the legislation on Olympic coins with specific authority. That was not what I was asking about in committee that day.
At that same meeting I asked the Master of the Mint if he was looking for more specific direction from this kind of a bill. I said:
If the Mint has already projected a plan for producing and marketing coins, then why can we not hear about it? I think that is the problem that faces us with this bill.
The Master of the Mint replied:
There is no plan because there was no act of parliament on the basis of which we could produce a gold coin in advance.
He stressed the fact that they needed to be able to plan for up to five years. He went on to say, and I quote:
If we knew in advance that we could have a gold coin program for five years to come, we could plan in advance for themes for the five yeas to come,-
The point is that parliament could have considered a bill which could have given the Mint authority to conduct a program over a period of years. However, we are being asked to approve a bill which gives authority to the governor in council to approve any kind of coin program. It is true the government has indicated it would be able to live with a time limit. In fact, the time limit will be something less than three years if this bill and amendment are approved.
Planning is obviously lacking both on the part of the government and the minister. I want to refer to the minister's remarks. He stated today that obviously further planning is needed and that there are further details that need to be laid out in order to get this program going.
I do not think hon. members, particularly those on this side, can approve a bill which states that the power of parliament will be taken away and given to cabinet on important matters such as issuing coins of any denomination, and in any quantity, all the way down the line. The minister said today that he cannot tell us the government's plans in the precise confines we would like to know about them. If the minister is not able to tell us, we cannot expect the Master of the Mint to tell us what is going on.
I want to refer again to the meeting of April 27. In answer to a question, the parliamentary secretary stated with regard to the planning for a program that the government had had in mind to introduce a Mint Act and possibly some amendments to the Currency and Exchange Act. We now have another

example of the government changing its mind. The parliamentary secretary stated at that time, and I quote:
As time seemed to be going past, what was lifted out of that package was this bill, which was intended to give the authority to get on with the commemorative coins and protect that market, with the idea that the more in-depth discussion you are talking about, Mr. Clarke, would happen at a later date.
I can understand that, but I do not really like it. I asked:
Is there no more specific plan the Mint could give us now as to the plans, broad plans, they have for this program?
The Master of the Mint replied:
-we do not have a plan now, but it would not be a problem to prepare such a plan because we know how many coins we sold in 1977.
I hope that is an adequate illustration of the fact that we should give very serious consideration to whether this bill should be supported at this stage because of what it will do to the power of parliament with regard to issuing coins, to the Mint which is not able to plan, as well as to the cabinet which will have to decide what will be issued under this bill, because that really has not been decided at this time.
One indicator that more planning is needed before, not after, this bill is passed is that only one theme has been determined, national unity. That is to be the theme of the first coin. The Master of the Mint indicated that it had not yet been decided what other themes might be used down the road.
I cannot imagine how a national unity theme could be depicted on a coin. We did not hear anything about that in committee. How will it look to outsiders? After all, these coins are aimed at the outside market, not the Canadian market. How will it appear to the purchasers of these coins to have Canada telling the world, by some theme on a coin, that Canada has a national unity problem? After ten years under the direction of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) it should be obvious that we do have a national unity problem, but I am not sure I want to see Canada's problems aired abroad on the face of a coin. I find this theme an objectionable one. And to me it seems strange the government should want to advertise the fact that there is a unity problem here by making unity the theme of a coin to be circulated in the world market.
Furthermore, the government has made no commitment with regard to the priority it would place on the issuance of the various coins in respect of which it is seeking our approval. My point is that the bullion coin program is one seen by the mining industry and by the government itself, according to speeches which have been made, as being the salient one. Yet neither the minister nor the parliamentary secretary in the committee was able to give us any assurance that the bullion program would be stressed. The Master of the Mint had certainly received no instructions from the government telling him which would be regarded as the primary program.
It is interesting to note that the industry, in its representations, stressed the number of jobs which would be created by the program which is proposed. I was interested to hear the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) expressing his support for the gold mining industry. I do not often hear hon.
May 8, 1978

members in that group to my left speaking as did the hon. member for Timiskaming today on behalf of the gold mining industry, but I can understand his doing so because there are a lot of people in his area who are employed by this industry.
It appears the industry was told by the government that this was a non-partisan bill and given the impression that their cause would be helped if they were able to get around and visit as many members of parliament as possible to seek support for the measure. There is certainly no lack of support on this side of the House for the gold mining industry, but we must take into account that the bill has implications which may be more serious than the question of jobs in the gold mining industry, for example, the request to delegate these additional powers to cabinet.
I should like to deal with the job aspect for a few moments and see how the industry's submissions stand up to examination. In committee, on April 24, I was asking about the creation of jobs at the Mint as well as outside in connection with related products such as blanks and cases, as well as in mining and related industries. The representative of the industry was asked why the gold had to be made in the form of a coin. He replied that if there were to be sales in a foreign market the object had to be a coin. A coin could not be produced by a private corporation; it had to be produced by a government. The representative of the mining industry went on to explain that it would be unsatisfactory to issue a medallion because such a product would be dutiable on entry, say, into the United States. The amount of duty was later identified as being 17.5 per cent. A medallion would not be the equivalent of a bullion coin.
We have heard from my hon. friend from York-Simcoe about the degree of fluctuation in the price of gold. The value of a gold medallion could vary widely, but in the case of a $100 gold coin the "downside risk" is a lot less than in the case of a gold medallion. The language of the trade describes such a coin as an investment vehicle. I asked why the effect on employment would be greater if a coin were issued, and why a similar effect could not be obtained from minting medallions. The representative of the industry replied that the gold mines could not sell enough of their production at a price which would make a profit-

the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act. We know that the act very generously and, I think, wisely, provides for the accommodation of mothers prior to and immediately after their terms of pregnancy. That is very good, progressive, and reflective of a concerned society. However, it has always struck me as strange that we have not given consideration to adoptive mothers who bring infant children into their homes. We have not given to these people the attention we perhaps could have.
While bringing an adoptive infant into the home does not necessarily have the same physical stresses of natural motherhood, the adoptive mother, nevertheless, is under some emotional strain. If it is a first adopted child, the situation in the home is not unlike that of the situation in which a child who is the result of natural childbirth is brought into the home. The same care is required, and both mother and father have the same concern for the adopted child. However, we make no provision for the adoptive parent to have the time at home necessary to adapt properly to the new member of the family and to assist that child in adapting to its new environment.
I raised this matter in 1976 and again in 1977. All I have been asking is that the House give some consideration to amending the act to extend benefits to mothers who adopt infants. Perhaps I should qualify my proposal by saying that I do not think this should apply to people who adopt children over a year or a year and a half old. It should perhaps be restricted to parents who adopt children 18 months old or younger, or 12 months old or younger. However, adoptive parents adopting infant children should be extended the same benefits we afford to natural parents.
I raised this matter on March 21, 1977, and also on November 22, 1976. In January of 1976 I wrote to the then minister responsible for the Unemployment Insurance Commission. I received a reply from his departmental assistant in which he attempted to justify the government's stance on the ground of the differing voluntary and involuntary nature of adoption and pregnancy. So that hon. gentlemen will be aware of my continuing concern I would like to quote the crux of his argument as follows:
The payment of benefits to major-attachment claimants who have incurred an interruption of earnings due to sickness or pregnancy, is in recognition of the principle that these conditions, generally involuntary-
I wonder what the mothers and wives of today think of that phrase.
-cause a claimant to be incapable of work. As a generality, the adoptive parents cannot be said to have incurred an involuntary condition which renders him or her incapable of work, as the adoption was, in fact, an act at the discretion of the parents and, under these circumstances, it is not possible to consider the granting of benefits.
I said then and I say today that I think that reeks of bureaucratic idiocy. It makes no sense at all. I want to make the point that that is an argument against the extension to adoptive mothers of provisions similar to those extended to natural mothers. It is wrong, and I think this House would like to indicate to the government that it should be corrected.
We have an opportunity for a few minutes this afternoon to address ourselves to this. I hope there will be comments from

the other side of the House. I want only to commend this motion to the House. I have dealt with it in this chamber on at least two previous occasions, and my comments, feeling, and attitude about this discrepancy have not changed in the two or three years during which we have been confronted with it. Having had a couple of years to consider this matter, and considering that this proposal has the support of hon. gentlemen such as the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) and others, perhaps we could persuade the appropriate people to consider extending this simple yet meaningful and very much desired help.
I myself am an adoptive parent. Adoptive parents are very real people who have very real feelings and concerns for the children who come into their homes and lives. When there is an adoption, there is an interruption of work. Perhaps it is not involuntary as it is in the case of pregnancy, but I suggest that it is involuntary in the sense that families which want children and which cannot have them are in fact not doing something voluntary. They are responding to natural instincts. Indeed, of those hon. members in this chamber who are adoptive parents it might even be said that they responded to very deep seated and unselfish urges.
I ask those who follow me to look at the simplicity of this motion. A very simple amendment could be dealt with quite quickly. This is just a resolution but, if the House saw fit, an appropriate and positive conclusion of this debate in general support of the resolution might just cause the government to consider the matter. There are thousands and thousands of families in Canada which would appreciate such a measure. In many instances it is needed, and the need is not superficial. It is real.
Without prolonging the debate or repeating the points I made in previous debates with respect to this matter I would like to commend this motion to hon. members and to suggest to them that it is a further indication of our concern for our society and the people who are in it, and particularly for those who want to bring into their homes infant children and to make them part of their families and lives. It seems only fair that the benefits made available for the involuntary act should be made available for the voluntary act.
