Mr. Speaker, the payment of unemployment insurance to adoptive parents is a matter regularly reviewed by the commission which has been considering that complex and multifaceted problem for about six years. Let us see, for example, how society looks upon adoption. We must point out immediately that the number of children put up for adoption has dropped appreciably in recent years because single mothers are more inclined to keep their child. In short, while the number of children has declined, that of parents who would like to adopt has increased. Today a single parent can adopt a child, something which was unthinkable some ten years ago.
The phenomenon of adoption has also changed. The adoption of older children who often have physical or emotional problems is no longer an unusual occurrence nowadays. Therefore, the needs of those children and their adoptive parents are no longer the same. They also have changed during the past 15 years.
Today most adoptive parents earn an adequate annual income. It is an important criterion in the eyes of adoption agencies. This is why it is good to question the idea of supporting these families financially.
Before deciding on the advisability of giving maternity benefits to the persons who adopt a child, let us recall that the main objective of unemployment insurance is to give temporary support to any person who loses his or her insurable employment. To obtain this temporary help, namely unemployment insurance benefits, the person must look actively for a job, except of course if the work stoppage is due to illness or pregnancy. So, are eligible to this temporary financial help those persons who lose their jobs, who are unable to work or who try to find a job or those who are physically unable to work for a certain period of time.
That is the main objective of unemployment insurance. Does it meet the needs of the adoptive parent? Does the adoption of a child imply automatically that the parent will have to stay out of work? I think the answer is no. Generally speaking, to draw unemployment insurance benefits, one has to be able to work and to be available to this end. An adoptive parent can sometimes meet these two primary requirements. For example, it is possible that the child may need constant care from one of both parents. The parent who goes out of the labour market is, according to the Unemployment Insurance Act, able to work but not available to this end. Furthermore, a mother who has a baby is considered as being physically apt to work. Consequently, if the adoptive parent is not available for work according to the law, he or she cannot draw unemployment insurance benefits. Those two major conditions, that is ability and availability, enable the authorities to determine unequivocally the entitlement of a claimant.
May 8, 1978

The concept of extending benefit eligibility to adoptive parents is to be commended. However, in so doing we would be paying people who have voluntarily left the labour force and who are able to work. Their motives cannot be compared to the physical and uncontrollable reasons that I mentioned earlier. It is certain that adoptive parents may have to stay at home to take care of the new child. However, adoption agencies always explain to the parents the needs of the child to be adopted. Therefore, during the adoption process, the parents are aware that one of them will have to stay at home. Their decision is voluntary.
By paying them benefits, the government would establish a precedent and undermine the basic principles of the unemployment insurance plan. Someone who is physically able but not available to work for reasons other than those which concern the labour force could then receive unemployment insurance. Availability would no longer be a condition of eligibility for those who can explain why they do not meet this condition.
I would like to emphasize that I am not attacking the idea of adoption. Adopting a child is a very laudable social action through which many children can become part of a family. It gives the possibility to many adoptive parents of knowing the joy of raising children. Moreover, this is not a matter of saying whether we are for or against some sort of assistance for adoptive parents. The Unemployment Insurance Act was simply not designed for this purpose.
Some adoptive parents need financial assistance and others do not. In both cases, the decisions to adopt a child and to leave the labour market go together and must be made voluntarily. We must also remember that the main purpose of the unemployment insurance plan is to give temporary assistance to anyone who loses his insurable employment to allow him to find new employment quickly.
Canada's employment picture is not very good. The unemployment insurance program is not a welfare program. It is not designed to cover all social needs. I suggest it would be unwise to grant unemployment insurance benefits to adoptive parents because they must stay home for a given period of time. Since maternity benefits do exist, it is understandable that some would like these benefits also to be paid to adoptive parents. Yet this would contradict the basic principles of this program. Women collect maternity benefits only because they are physically unable to work. Adoptive parents are physically capable of working even though adoption agencies may require that they temporarily give up their employment.
The unemployment insurance program should not become a substitute for other social aid programs. The program is not designed to meet all the income needs of Canadians. I have no doubt that adoptive parents might need some form of financial support. Their problems can even be more complex than those of natural parents. I am, however, opposed to this motion because in my opinion unemployment insurance is not the proper instrument to help them.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to speak on the motion of the hon. member even though I will not be speaking in support of it. The notion of paying unemployment insurance benefits to adoptive parents, in much the same way that benefits are now paid to workers unemployed due to pregnancy, is not new. However, unemployment insurance was designed to provide adequate, short-term income maintenance for workers who, for reasons beyond their control, are unemployed, capable of work and available and actively searching for work, or temporarily physically incapable of work.
Unemployment insurance, then, is for workers who are unemployed for reasons beyond their control. While collecting unemployment insurance, unemployed claimants must actively look for work unless they are physically unable to do so. Adopting a child is a deliberate, conscious decision. The parent of an adopted child, although physically able to work, would not be available and would not be actively looking for a job. To give people in this situation unemployment insurance benefits would be to distort the purpose of the whole unemployment scheme.

speechtext:
As most of us know, in the adoption process the particular needs of the child are outlined ahead of time to the prospective parents. If there is the need for one parent to remain in the home, this is known almost from the beginning.
If the parents work outside the home and decide to adopt a child and this requires one parent to leave the labour force, the adoption becomes a conscious decision that one parent leave the labour force. It becomes a responsibility that the parents assume jointly. The conscious element in the parents' decision to adopt puts the matter outside the principles and the scope of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
If the government were to consider giving unemployment insurance benefits to adopting parents, a precedent would be set that would distort the purpose of unemployment insurance. With this precedent, why not pay benefits to any capable but unavailable insured person whose unemployment was caused by conditions other than the labour market? Using this reasoning process, I can envisage thousands of persons deciding to be unavailable for work for what they, in their own minds, saw as good reason. They would argue that they were entitled to unemployment insurance on the grounds that their decision made them unavailable for work. The implications of this are obvious and too far-reaching. I must emphasize here that the issue before us is not the process of adoption itself. Adoption

May 8, 1978
Adoption Benefits
plays a vital role in our society, providing good homes for children who are disadvantaged or parentless. It gives childless couples the chance to experience the joy of parenthood. The issue at stake is not to decide whether adopting parents should get some form of special aid from the government either. The point in question is whether unemployment insurance is the appropriate vehicle for such assistance. In other words, my concern is not whether adopting parents may need some kind of support. There will be those who will and those who will not. My concern is to retain intact the principles of the unemployment insurance program in this country. These principles have remained essentially the same over the nearly 40 years since the first Unemployment Insurance Act was passed.
Unemployment insurance is not a welfare program. We are all aware that unemployment is a problem in Canada today. But to use the unemployment insurance legislation as a sort of catch-all instrument to cure our social ills, however valid these needs may be, would be unwise.
Because the unemployment insurance program pays maternity benefits, I can understand people assuming that a parallel exists between that and the payment of support to adopting parents. Once it is understood, though, that maternity benefits are paid because of physical incapacity to work, the parallel disappears.
At a time when we are all concerned about unemployment, we must not attempt to force the unemployment insurance program to encompass areas it was not designed to cover. We must not use it as a substitute for other social aid programs. I do not agree with those who see unemployment insurance as the general aid mechanism through which the federal government can solve virtually any legitimate social need of Canadians. Unemployment insurance is a type of social insurance and not the answer to Canadians' income needs, regardless of their nature. If we were to remove the link between unemployment insurance and the labour force and give workers the right voluntarily to remain out of work, we would completely defeat long-established principles.
In discussing the principles of the Unemployment Insurance Act, the words "capability" and "availability" are crucial. Regular unemployment insurance claimants must be both capable of work and available for work. They must also search actively for a job. In the case of claimants on maternity benefits, the person is considered to be incapable of working because of her pregnancy. Maternity claimants do not have to prove that they are available for work because of this incapacity to work. Adopting parents fit into neither category. An adopting parent who has withdrawn from the labour force is physically capable of work, but not available for work.
Under the terms of the Unemployment Insurance Act, then, this parent is not entitled to any benefit. To pay benefit to adoptive parents-laudable though this may seem in principle-would be to pay people who, although capable of work, have made a conscious decision to withdraw from the labour
force. As I stated earlier, this would set a precedent that would erode the very base of unemployment insurance in Canada.
I said earlier that unemployment insurance is not welfare. Insurance spreads financial losses over the large numbers who face the risk. The benefits, paid out when financial loss occurs, are met from a fund made up of premiums paid by contributors. Welfare, on the other hand, is payable on a condition, such as need. Need is a subjective thing and it changes over time. Need cannot be financed using actuarially-determined premiums, as insurance is. This is why welfare benefits are usually financed from general taxation.
Insurance benefits, of course, are financed from pooling premiums. For unemployment insurance, premiums paid by employers and employees are calculated to cover the basic cost of benefits, including administrative cost. This is actuarially sound and meets insurance principles. To attempt to distort an insurance scheme so that it covers both the contingency of unemployment and the element of need inherent in social welfare programs would mean weakening the whole structure of the labour market and its relationship with jobs and people in this country.
Late last summer, this House passed amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act in Bill C-27. These changes were evidence of the government's continuing desire to respond, within the framework of unemployment insurance principles, to the needs of Canadian workers. May I add at this point that it is my opinion that we should be seriously considering introducing additional amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act so that persons drawing benefits which are a considerable drain on the economy and who, in my opinion, are not entitled to them should be excluded from those presently listed as unemployed. I refer specifically to persons who would ordinarily be on contract for periods of six, eight or nine months and who now are able to draw unemployment benefits for the remaining months of the year. I speak specifically of classes such as golf professionals and others who up to a certain point in time used to consider themselves fortunate to earn enough income in eight months to last for twelve but who in my opinion are now drawing from the taxpayer moneys to which they should not be entitled.
One of the most significant of the changes made in Bill C-27 was what is called the variable entrance requirement. This amendment made eligibility for unemployment insurance dependent on the rate of unemployment in the region of the country where the claimant ordinarily lives. What this means in practice is that the worker in a region of high unemployment would need fewer weeks of insurable unemployment than the worker in a region of relatively low unemployment. But let me stress here again that this kind of response to conditions in the labour market was done within the framework of the Unemployment Insurance Act and the principles enshrined in it.
While I am on my feet, Mr. Speaker, when the department makes an error, such as it did recently in using a wrong calculation which resulted in an overpayment of $4.3 million to some 15,000 claimants, it is my personal opinion that this is

May 8, 1978

not the fault of the claimants, and under such circumstances the department should accept its responsibility and absorb that loss.

I think it would be fair to say that many adopting families have adequate means of income. The Children's Aid Societies are very careful in selecting parents for the adoption process and income is one of the criteria used in their decision. Because of this, many adopting families are in the middle or upper income range.
That is not to say that we should not be thinking of some programs to aid parents who do not have the income to adopt children and who should have the benefit and privilege of children in their home. What 1 am arguing this afternoon is that the unemployment insurance scheme is not the vehicle to be used. That is not to say there may not be a need for some form of financial support for the parents, probably as a provincial area of responsibility, although with our difficulties today perhaps we should not be emphasizing what is provincial and what is federal. But a deliberate decision must be made by adoptive parents, presumably after discussions have taken place with the Children's Aid people on the needs of the child and the parents' ability to provide these needs. So it seems to me that unemployment insurance is not the appropriate place to look for aid in these circumstances.
This is not the first time this House has considered the proposal to pay unemployment insurance to a parent who adopts a child. The issue has been raised on other occasions and the arguments for and against have been aired. Mr. Speaker, I do not want to appear to discredit the adoption process in any way. As I mentioned earlier, adoption does play an important role in finding homes for orphaned and disadvantaged children.
Personally, I think we should take every measure to make it possible for those parents who are in the unfortunate position of not having children of their own to be able to adopt. Adoption plays an important role in finding homes for orphans and disadvantaged children. It gives people who are childless the chance to experience the joys and the rewards of parenthood. The give and take of parent-child relationships is extended through this adoption process and society as a whole benefits. I have no argument against this process. I applaud it most warmly.
Neither do I dispute that adoptive parents may very well need some form of support in their very worth-while endeavours. Indeed, in many ways I believe the role of adoptive parent is often more difficult than that of natural parent. Those parents who decide to contribute so much of themselves in the adoption process are greatly to be admired. But I find myself unable to support this motion to pay unemployment insurance benefits to adoptive parents because I firmly believe the Unemployment Insurance Act is not the right place to provide this kind of assistance. There must be other places to look for help of this kind, not tied firmly to existing insurance principles and not strictly based on capability to work.

Mr. Speaker, I was not going to speak to this motion today because I had hoped it might get passed and I did not want to contribute to the so-called talking-out process. However, that process seems to be in full flight, so I may as well say a few words.
I am prompted to do so mainly by the remarks of the last two speakers. It is rather interesting to note today that the only speech we have had on this motion from the Conservatives was a Liberal speech, and the last two speeches from the Liberal side have been Tory speeches. I suppose at election time things like that can happen. My hon. friend who just took his seat and the member who preceded him both spoke as though unemployment insurance is based on some basic principle that has never been tampered with or breached at all. I can say that when the program started the idea was that unemployment insurance was to be paid only in cases where there was no work and only to persons who were available for that work.
In the early years when we argued that it should be paid to people who were not at work because they were ill, we were told that would violate the basic principle of the Unemployment Insurance Act. After a while the principle was modified slightly and the law changed so that if a person was collecting unemployment insurance because there was no work and then took sick afterwards, his unemployment insurance benefits were continued. Then after a period of time we said that if we paid unemployment insurance to certain persons who were sick, why not to those who had to leave their work because they were sick, and finally that category was added. Of course, for a long time it was argued that we could not bend the provisions for persons who needed unemployment insurance because of maternity, but we eventually breached that and decided that that too was a legitimate reason for being away from work.
My hon. friend who has just taken his seat, the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert), suggests that if we go a step further and allow unemployment insurance benefits to be paid to adoptive parents, we will be opening the way to anyone who says "I am not available, I want to go on a holiday" or to someone to say "I want to write a thesis". I suggest this whole matter is under our control.
There is a relationship between the process of adopting children and the process of having children. Most of us in this place do not know what it is like to bear children, but there are a few who can tell us about the experience. It seems to me there are times when natural mothers can work almost up to the time of childbirth and then are able to go back to work right after. I have known of other cases of parents adopting children who have gone through such an emotional experience

that they needed to stay home. So I suggest this attempt to draw a hard and fast line really does not match the situation, and it certainly does not match the fine sentiments about our being a society that ought to encourage home building through the adopting process. So, Mr. Speaker, the arguments I have listened to do not carry any weight with me. I should still like to see this motion passed.
Incidentally, my hon. friend from Vaudreuil said that he should like to see something done to encourage the adoption of children but he does not want to see it done through the unemployment insurance route. Even if we passed this motion, it would not legislate anything. It would just express the opinion that something ought to be done for adoptive parents. True, it suggests it might be done through unemployment insurance, but it would give the government a lead to do some thinking about this issue. subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO AUTHORIZE ISSUANCE OF CERTAIN GOLD COINS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as it came up to five o'clock, I was explaining the severe reservations that we on this side have concerning this bill. Primarily, the bill will remove the power from parliament and give it to the governor in council to make rulings as far as the gold coinage of Canada is concerned. Also, I spoke about the lack of planning the government have shown in introducing a bill of this sort when the concept of what it is they plan to do has not been spelled out.
Just before five o'clock I had reached the point where I was talking about the production of jobs, what the program was going to do and how the mining industry representative had said to the committee that at the moment the industry cannot sell enough of its production at a price that enables it to make a profit. They want the price of gold to be determined in world
May 8, 1978

markets. This program will provide additional demand. They expect this demand will lead to an orderly upward movement in the price of gold. He stressed the word "orderly".
The problem is that the government has not given any commitment to the production of the bullion coin, simply to the production of the medallion. It has been adequately demonstrated that the medallion will not have any particular value from the point of view of the mining industry. The demand for a medallion will be rather poor. There are a couple of very good reasons for that.
I want to illustrate before going on that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) had some very severe reservations concerning the production of a gold coin for sale as a piece of gold. In a letter written by the Minister of Finance in December 1977 referring to the proposal for a gold bullion coin, he said:
First of all, it would seem to me that the term "coin" should not be used in this instance.
The production and sale of tokens whose selling price would be related to the commodity value of gold would be acceptable, he said. He then said:
We would want to ensure that the tokens were not marketed with any implied guarantees by the government as to future value.
Of course, this is why the gold coin idea will sell, because it has a stop loss value of $100 Canadian, if that is the amount decided on by the government. The minister went on in his letter:
We would want it clearly understood by potential buyers that these tokens were not legal tender and had no monetary value.
Of course, there has been a grave danger since then because they would have a monetary value. They would be put out by the government through the Mint.
The minister summarized his views by saying:
-while I have no objection to a private manufacturer producing and marketing gold tokens, I would not wish to see these described as "gold bullion coins" which might have an implied monetary value or guarantee on the part of the government.
We can see that the government has made many changes in planning and that the planning has many deficiencies. Parliament is being asked, in approving this bill, to countenance aiding and abetting those who would like to move their investments in gold across international borders without attracting duty. I mentioned this afternoon that the rate of duty in the United States would be 17.5 per cent in the case of somewhat similar products. I raised this matter in committee on April 27. The Master of the Mint had admitted that the value of the coins bore no relation to the face value. The value of the gold was what counted, just as the value of the medallion would fluctuate with the price of gold. But if the government of Canada lends its name, investors are able to buy them with a stop loss value and thereby circumvent duties imposed by other countries on valuables moved across their borders.
I refer again to the minutes of the committee for April 27. A question was raised on that occasion having to do with sales
Currency and Exchange Act
tax on coins issued by the government. If one takes ten $20 bills to a bank and exchanges them for two $100 bills there is, of course, no imposition of sales tax. The idea of a sales tax imposed on the exchange of one combination of notes for another is ridiculous, I would be the first to agree. But the government allows provincial governments to levy provincial sales tax on legal tender. I am referring specifically to other coins produced by the Mint. In the committee I expressed the point as follows:
What concerns me is the matter of sales tax on these coins within Canada at the moment, particularly the gold coins commemorating the Silver Jubilee of Queen Elizabeth II. When one goes into a bank and buys a $50 bill or a $100 bill there is no suggestion that sales tax is payable and there is no question that $100 Silver Jubilee coins are legal tender; yet, when one buys them, particularly in British Columbia, one must pay the 7 per cent provincial tax. Of course, the defence given is that, to use the minister's words:
... the determination of what goods are subject to provincial sales tax is the responsibility of the provincial governments.
I was quoting from the minister's letter to me. To continue the quotation:
The minister presumes that
... the provinces imposing tax are doing so on the basis that these items are considered to be commodities when traded and not legal tender. As to why such a levy should be allowed, I can only state that to date the courts have not found that the provinces cannot impose these levies.
I would ask hon. members to compare this situation, in which the federal government accepts the position of provincial sales tax on Canadian legal tender, with the provision in the budget established some four weeks ago on April 10 when the cabinet found it was not too difficult to get all the ministers of finance of the provinces, or at least the overwhelming majority of them, to agree that concerted action be taken at Ottawa's behest. The result, as we know, is that provincial sales taxes were reduced.
In summary, we have many things to complain about in this bill and not very much to agree with. We support the intention to provide jobs in the mining industry and in certain areas outside, including the Mint. But the measure has implications which go beyond this. There is the aspect involving the further erosion of parliamentary powers-the emasculation of this institution. Then again, by voting for this bill, we would be aiding and abetting people who want to move gold across international borders duty-free. All this, together with the general lack of planning and the fact that the government has refused to commit itself to going ahead with the bullion program, is not good enough. I hope the minister and his colleagues will reconsider their approach before the question comes to the final vote.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO AUTHORIZE ISSUANCE OF CERTAIN GOLD COINS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this little bill involving the minting of commemorative coins, tokens and so on is not one of great importance, in my opinion, and we might be better occupied dealing with some of the tax bills flowing from the recent budget. But it does give rise to certain difficulties. The government itself does not seem very clear as to its objectives.
The government would like authority to mint coins of a commemorative nature, for example, coins marking the 25th

May 8, 1978
Currency and Exchange Act
anniversary of the Coronation or the holding of the Olympic Games. Such coins would be limited in face value but the face value would be much greater than the gold in the coin is worth. The minister has informed us that the governors of the Mint have suggested a unity theme for one proposed issue. In my view this is a stupid proposal. Other speakers in this debate have pointed out that presumably the country is unified already and that the issuance of a gold coin is not likely to appeal to many as being a very practical manifestation of unity.
As things are, parliament is the sole body, as I understand it, which can authorize the minting of coins for a particular purpose such as the commemoration of the Olympics. I am inclined to think that this authority should remain with parliament. It would seem as though the government really intends to run a type of lottery, and I would place many of these proposed coins in that category.
By minting coins such as this we are, in essence, competing with private mints, and I am not sure that that is the right thing to do. I believe that parliament should retain the authority to authorize a commemorative gold coin, but only under certain circumstances. This should not be given up to the whims of the cabinet, and especially not the present minister. The problem of unity is ongoing and will certainly not be solved by minting such a coin. I am more interested in a gold bullion coin. The mining industry has pushed the idea of a concept based on the South African Kruger rand, which is a coin bought at the price of gold of the day plus a small amount for minting and distribution. It is somewhat of an anomaly that nations around the world are getting rid of gold as a monetizing agent-in other words, attempting to demonetize gold and remove it as a standard. Gold has been a standard, I suppose, for 5,000 years or more, and gold has retained its value.
While governments may be demonetizing gold, people are turning to gold as a hedge against inflation. While governments tend to rely on the International Monetary Fund, individuals are buying gold to deal with inflation. It is interesting that at the present time the United States has something like S55 billion in gold based on $180 an ounce, or $270 million in troy ounces. However, much of it is impure. It is called coin melt and has a gold content of only about 90 per cent. West Germany has about $50 billion worth of gold at present day prices, France, $17 billion and Switzerland and Italy, $14 billion, while Canada and Britain each have only about $3.6 billion. It interesting to note that the most desired currency in the world is the Swiss franc, which is, relatively, the most heavily gold-backed currency in the world.
Incidentally, it has been suggested that the gold reserves of the central banks of the leading countries now amount to nearly $180 billion at present day market prices. It is an important reserve because it exceeds SDER's on special drawing rights from the International Monetary Fund by some 1,800 per cent. So although on the one hand governments talk

about demonetizing gold, on the other hand gold is now one of the biggest reserves in banks throughout the world.
Many people are now interested in acquiring gold in the form of coins such as the Kruger rand. It is interesting that in their testimony outside experts quoted the fact that the only refugees from Viet Nam who were able to bring in valuables were those who had gold in some form or another. So it is a form of savings. It is something we can carry with us. It has been used over the centuries as a valuable commodity which can be moved.
It seems to me that with the inflation we have gold has value. It had a value in the past, even 5,000 years ago, and it continues to have a value. Even if governments do not wish to accumulate gold any more and wish to demonetize it, the mere fact that our citizens want to accumulate it makes the minting of a gold bullion coin very practical. I mentioned that the Swiss franc, which is, relatively speaking, the largest gold-backed currency for a small country, is in demand, and it seems to me practical that citizens should hold gold in coins, bullion coins or in some other form. That would be endorsed by the public, and would, in the long run, strengthen and stabilize our credit and financial institutions. The present monetary system is based on paper and confidence in it. At this time it shows serious signs of erosion. There are violent currency fluctuations.
All over the world people in many countries are buying Kruger rands. It is interesting that in January of 1978 some
700,000	units of Kruger rands were sold. That represents something like 700,000 ounces. In February some 600,000 were sold. The financial pages are full of articles indicating that gold is increasing in popularity. People are buying gold shares, gold bullion or gold stocks. If a Canadian bullion coin was available, Canadians would likely buy a few. In addition, markets in the United States and West Germany would be prime for gold bullion coins.
It has been suggested that the coins should be half-ounce or one ounce. Some studies have indicated that international markets would probably absorb one million one-ounce gold coins a year. That would still only amount to one and one-half month's Kruger rand sales. However, it would contribute to the international currency market. An increasing number of investors of very modest means are placing some of their assets in gold as an ultimate hedge against any drastic altering of existing relationships among major currencies. Indeed, some economists are suggesting that gold is one of the best holdings with which to provide a hedge against severe inflation. Some have suggested that perhaps one quarter of one's assets should be held personally in the form of gold, so it does not seem as though there is any disadvantage to minting a gold bullion coin.
However, unfortunately the government has not seen fit to say whether it is in favour of a gold bullion coin. There was talk about that in committee, but we did not hear the government say that it expected to mint one. I think that a gold bullion coin would meet with general approval and would be a major thrust in creating stability in the industry. It would
May 8, 1978

provide more jobs. In the 1930's gold mines produced income and jobs for a relatively large number of miners when other mines were at a low ebb. As I understand it, gold mines are relatively labour intensive, so more jobs are created by a given amount of capital investment in gold mines than in other types of mines.
We in Canada are encouraged to export more, but we often export goods which are not very competitive. We have heard about our exports in manufactured goods. We have heard that the Export Development Corporation has to underwrite some 42 per cent of capital goods exported from Canada to destinations other than on the North American continent. If we were to export gold bullion coins, job creation would be accelerated because of increased mining activity. By exporting coins we would be exporting finished products. That would fulfil the wishes of those who suggest that raw products should be upgraded before being exported.
It has been suggested that as we are the third largest gold producing nation in the world we would not need to be financed by the Export Development Corporation because there is a solid market for gold coins. If the market holds up to what has been projected in studies, it would indicate that all our present day gold production would be used up, and presumably we would bring into play substantial amounts from other mines. The Mint would benefit from the minting of the bullion coins and should return a modest profit.
It seems to me that it is much more desirable to mint a gold bullion coin, which people wish to have as a hedge against inflation, even if governments do not always agree as to its value, than to run what I consider to be a kind of lottery on commemorative coins. Many people, including myself, believe that a $100 gold piece contains $100 worth of gold, but in reality it does not. The value of gold would have to be inflated many times over before it reached the face value of the coin, as we realized when we studied this bill.
In conclusion, I certainly support the minting of a bullion coin, but I am most unhappy at the fact that the government seems to prefer minting a token unity coin in attempting to supply the market when a bullion coin would go a long way toward providing incentives to our gold mining industry, resulting in over-all stability for our miners. I believe that the United States and West Germany would provide markets for the minted bullion coin and that individuals in the western world who wished to buy gold as a hedge against inflation would also be interested in buying the minted coin.
In view of the fact that the government has not been clear with regard to what it wishes to do in this situation, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker):
That Bill C-39, to amend the Currency and Exchange Act, be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs for the purpose of reconsidering the method of authorizing the issuance of gold coins and in particular gold bullion coins.

Mr. Speaker, that is about as phony a point of order as the points the hon. member made in committee, which were very phony. As I was attempting to say before I was so rudely interrupted by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre, we have some very genuine concerns about the impact of this bill upon certain sectors of the transportation industry.
I wish to review very briefly the position our party has taken on this bill. At second reading, we allowed the bill to advance to committee stage, at which time we were to call witnesses and study the details of the legislation and the impact it would have on the transportation industry. Implicit in that decision was the condition that various factors would then be taken into consideration, namely the impact this legislation would have upon other modes of transportation. We were concerned about what it would do with regard to distorting the competitive balance of the transportation industry.
Secondly, we were concerned about the provision of adequate safeguards to ensure that the measures of control and accountability of this corporation were enshrined in legislation. As well, we wanted to ensure that the funds which would supposedly be earmarked for improving the transportation system would in fact be earmarked for that purpose.
The third point we wanted to consider was whether this legislation was really needed and whether it would serve the benefit of the public interest.
Fourth, we were interested in examining the impact upon CNR, with recapitalization and without recapitalization, over a projected five-year period.
Having considered all these points, the members of our party concluded that this bill does not appear to be needed at the present time. In our view, it does not provide any degree of significant benefit to the national interest of Canada.
Second, notwithstanding the amendment that was accepted whereby the annual reports of the corporation will be automatically referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications, which is an improvement, in our
May 8, 1978

view this is not sufficient to adequately provide for the kind of control and accountability mechanisms that we seem to be aspiring to put in place with all Crown corporations.
Third, because the CNR have now proven to themselves, their shareholders and the country that they can turn the operations of the corporation into a profit on the basis of the existing financial structure, this implies that the current management team are in fact doing a very good job. The fact that they are turning the corporation around is very commendable. We, and I am sure all members of the House, join in commending the president of CNR, Dr. Robert Bandeen, and his management team on a job very well done. They have demonstrated that with sound management and good business practices the corporation can turn a profit on the basis of the existing financial structure.
It may be argued that the profit is not high enough to meet the cash requirement in terms of maintaining equipment, upgrading roadbeds and so on, but the fact remains there has been a major achievement on the basis of the existing structure. But most serious of all is the concern we have that the CN could disrupt the competitive balance in the transportation industry, particularly one of the major private sectors in the industry, that is to say, the trucking industry, and that the interest of the public would not be served as a result.
We feel strongly about this. The Canadian Trucking Association presented a detailed and comprehensive brief to the committee-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member is out in his constituency he is a great supporter of private enterprise, but back here in the Commons he is a doctrinaire socialist and nothing else. He speaks out of both sides of his mouth. He really does not support the trucking industry at all. He would like to see the whole trucking industry nationalized, as should be very clear from his utterances.
There are other considerations involved here, such as intentions on the part of the government which are not fully known at present, adjustments in the freight rates, the full impact of the removal of passenger service from the CN rail system and other consequences of government policy. For these reasons we believe the bill should not be proceeded with at this time.
Other speakers have dealt in detail with certain of our misgivings; I have myself expressed them in committee and I do not wish to cover the whole ground again. Nevertheless, I shall attempt to outline some of the circumstances which have led me to believe that it would be wise to defer this legislation. Mr. Speaker, we see this bill as an exercise in financial manipulation. When it was introduced, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said: Pass it, and it will save the taxpayers $100 million. As a result of the cross-examination which took place in the committee hearings we found out that this statement was utter nonsense. We can only conclude that, like the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), who
Railway Act
confirmed it, has become a master in the art of deceit. That statement about saving the taxpayers money is totally inaccurate and untrue. Anyone who cares to read the transcript of evidence will find that such is the case.
The other argument which was put forward concerned depreciation. That argument was almost as phony. If the depreciation had been assessed when we were told it should have been, perhaps at the time of the last recapitalization in 1952-or it could have been calculated on an annual basis thereafter-it would have had the effect of increasing the deficit by some $24 million annually. The CN would have ended up with a debt equity ratio of 1 per cent to 99 per cent, which would have been totally unacceptable.
What did happen was this. Throughout the course of the CN recapitalization of 1952 the net effect was to put the company on a debt equity basis comparable to that of the North American industry. It was at that time of the order of 65 per cent, which was reduced to some 40 per cent as a result of recapitalization. To achieve a debt equity ratio which would be similar to that of the North American industry we have, with the conversion of $808 million worth of debt which was considered unclaimed appreciation in the equity, here again improved the debt equity ratio from 62 per cent to 42 per cent.
The minister said this was required. I cite from page 2621 of Hansard:
However, the result of this long-standing obligation for the company to rely on loans for the bulk of its capital requirements has been a debt ratio of about 62 per cent compared with the rail industry average in North America of approximately 35 per cent, and about 35 per cent for the CPR in particular.
There, again, is a statement which is completely untrue. We found out during the committee hearings that there was no inherited debt to speak of after the 1952 recapitalization, so there really was not any long-standing obligation, as the minister stated. The evidence before the committee confirmed that all the inherited debt had been removed by 1952 and that the CN debt ratio was improved from about 65 per cent to 32 per cent, putting the company on the same basis as its major competitor, the CPR. So the depreciation argument is another argument which amounts to nothing more than hogwash.
What really happened after the 1952 recapitalization was that CN went on a spending spree. It purchased new equipment, bought out many trucking companies and engaged in the acquisition of many allied ventures. Then it found within ten years that it was back in the position it had occupied prior to recapitalization. Mr. Speaker, I am sure there are many private companies which would like to carry on their refinancing on such a basis. I would point out that the trucking industry, which the hon. member over there wants to nationalize, has to finance its requirements out of earnings, not from debt cancellation or the accrual of unused depreciation.
During the committee hearings I was talking about the ability or otherwise of Crown corporations to make a profit. I will mention two major hotels. First, the Macdonald Hotel in Edmonton, in 1973, showed a loss of $.1 million. It broke even in 1974, 1975 and 1976 and then showed a profit of $.1 million in 1977. So over a five-year period it was a break even

May 8, 1978
Railway Act
proposition. I suggest that there probably is not another hotel in the city of Edmonton with that kind of record. The same holds true for the Fort Garry, except it is a little worse: S.l million for 1973, $.1 million for 1974, $.2 million for 1975, $.2 million for 1976 and $.3 million for 1977, all losses. When we look at legislation like this, we are concerned about those kinds of things. Legislation like this really does nothing more than relieve the burden of debt from a Crown corporation which should do better.
I now come to what I refer to as the impact of the unknowns. Things which are taking place, either being enacted at the present time as a result of government policy or being contemplated, I submit will have a very significant impact upon the earning power and the operations of CN. I refer to branch line abandonment. Branch lines are constantly being abandoned, and branch lines will continue to be abandoned over the next 10, 15 or 20 years. This will place a heavier burden on farmers because the result of consolidation in the grain handling system will be more efficiency, and it will be easier for rail lines to move grain from country elevators to ports. However, it will entail much longer hauling distances for the average producer.
We have also talked about the withdrawal of passenger services. That too removes a liability or a deficit operation from the railway, some of which has been taken into consideration in the projected figures. We also have the prospect of an adjustment in the statutory freight rates, which the minister indicates will come about in due course and which will have a major and significant impact upon the earning potential of the CNR. There are fairly hefty grants from the government for railway rehabilitation and for the upgrading of tracks. The minister has indicated the figure of some $600 million going to both railways, the bulk of which will probably go to the CNR. We have budget relief measures which will accelerate depreciation on the purchase of equipment. There will be further purchases of hopper cars and continuing maintenance of a number of articles of rolling stock. Stated government policy provides for the payment of subsidies for the provision of any service which may not be economic, but which is deemed necessary in the public interest. We have the record of the CNR in terms of its improving its efficiency and its rationalization and in terms of cutting down its labour force, thereby improving productivity.
The total impact of these measures has not yet been felt, but I suggest that they will have a very major and significant impact upon the operations of the CNR from a cash generating point of view. The evidence in the committee suggested that taking into account some of these items, but not necessarily all of them, would result in CN's showing a profit of up to $294.2 million by the year 1981. Of course, this raises a couple of questions. First, can CN justify that level of profit? It is a Crown corporation. Second, we have to question what impact that much profit may have upon labour-management relations and particularly the negotiations which would take place between the unions and management. I think those two points

are very important, relevant and germane to this legislation. In addition to those two points the impact upon CN's competitors will, I suggest, be very substantial.
That brings me to the point which I consider to be the most important in this bill, and that is the impact upon other modes of transport, particularly those which are in direct competition with CN. Of course, once again I refer particularly to the trucking industry. I think that the minister and his colleagues have failed to recognize the legitimate concerns of the trucking industry. I think those concerns have been sloughed off. Notwithstanding, the minister has made assurances, and the officials of the CNR have made assurances, that these fears are unfounded. However, unfortunately the words expressed in the committee are not enshrined in the legislation. Therefore, any guarantees which may have been suggested or implied during consideration of this bill in committee are hollow and meaningless.
I believe that the Canadian trucking industry can say with some justification what it said in a statement which I wish to place on the record at this time. This statement was contained in the submission presented to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications by the Canadian Trucking Association. The Association said this:
CN management should be encouraged to compete in the marketplace on an equitable basis with private enterprise where transporation services can be self-supporting. We do not believe this can happen where the Crown-owned railway is given an overwhelming financial advantage. To be more specific, we are concerned that given enough financial leeway, CN management will again be tempted to try and buy their way into a self-contained empire of inter-connecting services where they would otherwise have to compete with other carriers for much of the interline business they would control. CN might decide that with one final cast of the dice they could revolutionize domestic transportation on a multi-modal basis and in the process effectively bury the competition.
The Association made the following concluding statement:
A condition precedent to passage of C-17 should be some kind of guarantee to parliament that CN will refrain from indulging in massive new investment schemes in an attempt to corner profitable domestic transportation markets while neglecting its responsibility to maintain, if not upgrade, services in those regions of the country where CN may be the dominant transportation undertaking and where return on investment is less attractive. Present procedures obviously aren't adequate.
I think those concerns are very fundamental and should be considered very seriously, because fundamental to sustaining an efficient and effective transportation system, the concept of equal treatment for all modes of transport by the government must certainly prevail. In this case I see this legislation discriminating against the trucking industry and, for that matter, the CPR.
I come to my final point. It is touched on in that final passage which I quoted, and it has to do with control and accountability and the assurance that the CNR will not be back to this parliament in 20 years for another recapitalization or another debt cancellation.

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-FORECAST OF UNEMPLOYMENT FIGURES AND REAL GROWTH
THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-FORECAST OF UNEMPLOYMENT FIGURES AND REAL GROWTH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question which is under debate this evening was one asked by myself of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) on April 21. My question was twofold. I asked the minister to indicate what was the estimated level of unemployment that had been used by his department in the April 10 budget which was tabled in the House; and secondly, what did he anticipate the real growth in the economy will be in the current year. Unfortunately the Minister of Finance indicated that it had not been the government's custom to indicate unemployment levels, and in effect he fudged that issue. So far as real growth is concerned, he stated that it would be approximately 5 per cent, which is slightly down from the earlier figures the minister had indicated for real growth.
I think it is particularly important when we are considering the economic plight of Canada that the government be pressed to indicate what they see in the coming years in terms of unemployment, real growth, inflation and the other standard indices. We cannot operate in a vacuum. Certainly to judge from past years, it is alarming to see the dramatic increases which occurred in Canada respecting unemployment. As far as numbers are concerned, unemployment has approximately tripled compared to the level in 1968. Inflation has more than doubled since 1968. Real growth has gone down. Government spending has soared. It is not enough for a budget to be introduced; it would also be helpful if the government would indicate what it sees for the unemployment level this year and in coming years.
The government has been inclined to rationalize its sad performance. It likes to pull various pictures out of the air to convince the public that it is doing a little better than most of us believe. For example, it is customary for the government to talk in terms of creation of jobs in Canada. It uses that as an excuse to justify the relatively high unemployment level in the country. In short, the government likes to say that it is not so much the fact that jobs have not been created as that the
[Mr. Forrestall.l
participation rate has been rising. Also it indicates that unemployment levels are higher than anticipated, and it is difficult to identify what unemployment levels will be in the coming months or years. That is not true.
If one takes a look at the past 30 months in Canada, it is startling to see since controls were imposed on our economy in October 1975 that inflation has gone up a full 4 per cent faster than in the United States. I compare our percentage to that in the United States because that country is our main trading partner and has no controls. On the other hand, real growth has been 4 per cent faster in the United States than in Canada. But most significantly, employment growth has been virtually nil in Canada, compared to 7 per cent in the United States. If Canada had had even half the rate of growth in the past 30 months of that in the United States, our unemployment levels would be down to the 5 per cent range. That is what we are talking about tonight. If the government are not anticipating unemployment at those levels, they owe the House and Canadians an explanation.
If we take a look at the past record, we find unemployment in Canada has risen from 5.3 per cent in 1974, to 6.9 per cent in 1975, to 7.1 per cent in 1976 and to 8.1 per cent on the average in 1977. The figure for 1977 indicates that there are
862,000	Canadians out of work. If that trend continues, it is startling to realize that by 1981 there will be 1,280,000 Canadians out of work and our unemployment level will be 10.6 per cent.
Dealing with real economic growth, on average the real economic growth has been 3.06 per cent since 1973. If that trend continues, it will mean the loss of a full three years of real growth by 1981. That will be tough to catch up with. Surely the government must indicate in more concrete terms where it is going. For example, in the "Economic Review" of April 1978, which was tabled approximately a week ago, at page 88 it is indicated that on a cyclically adjusted basis our deficit will be $4.4 billion in 1977 if various things are taken into account.
At committee we asked the minister what level of unemployment would have given the $4.4 billion deficit figure that they referred to. I was startled to find that they said 6.2 per cent unemployment would still leave a $4.4 billion deficit in this country. I want to thank the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) for asking this question in the adjournment debate because it gives me an opportunity to expand on the minister's answer which he gave on April 21. I am sure the hon. member will agree there was a great deal of confusion and misunderstanding generated by the perhaps less than clear
May 8, 1978

report of the most recent Conference Board numbers. It seems that the hon. member was one of many who have been captured by this confusion.
First of all, and most importantly, the Conference Board has not revised down its 4.5 per cent forecast for real growth as measured by the increase in real gross national product. Moreover, this 4.5 per cent forecast does not include the effects of the budget which everyone agrees will give a significant boost to real growth this year, nor does it include the Quebec budget which is also stimulative.
The 3.9 per cent figure referred to by the hon. member relates to the increase in real domestic product, not to g.n.p. What has happened is that the rates of increase for two quite different measures of output have been taken from the same forecast and reported as the same number. This confusion arose partly because the Conference Board released its national forecast, from which the 4.5 per cent g.n.p. number was taken, a few weeks before its provincial forecasts, from which the 3.9 per cent RDP number was taken. But the provincial forecasts in aggregate are consistent with the national forecast of 4.5 per cent real growth in g.n.p. It is my understanding that the Conference Board itself is quite concerned that this confusion has arisen. In fact, the Board is actively considering releasing the national forecast and the provincial detail simultaneously in the future precisely so that this mix-up will not arise again.
Secondly, the aggregation of unemployment rates from the Conference Board's provincial forecasts shows a national rate of 8.5 per cent compared to a rate of 8.4 per cent in their national forecast. The reason for this is again one of timing. The Conference Board's national forecast was prepared before the March labour force data was available while their provincial forecasts included this information. Despite very strong employment growth in that month, the unemployment rate rose as the participation rate increased by more than anyone had thought likely, the Conference Board included. The inclusion of the unexpectedly high March figure had the effect of raising the annual average marginally. Thus, there has not really been any revision in the forecast of the unemployment rate; rather, new past historical observations have been included in the 1978 base.
On the conceptual side, gross national product measures, as its name suggests, national product; that is, the boundary of production is drawn to include all of the production of Canadian factors of production irrespective of what country the production originates in. With the real domestic product, on the other hand, the boundaries of production are confined to the geographic boundaries of Canada, irrespective of whether the factors of production are Canadian or non-resident.

The government's proposals to amend the legislation governing railway freight rates are generally intended to promote a greater degree of fairness, both regionally and to shippers, while taking into account the financial need of the Canadian railways. The government envisages that Canadian railways should continue to exercise considerable freedom in establishing freight rates where competitive forces can be expected to protect the public interest. Nevertheless, because of the importance of the railway system to the national economy and the continued existence of some railway monopoly power in certain markets, it is proposed that the maximum and minimum rate provisions of the Railway Act should be strengthened.

New legislation would also address the problem of long-haul/short-haul rate differentials. This proposal is intended to modify an element of railway pricing which has been perceived as an example of unfair discrimination. At the same time, it will permit exceptions where a complete prohibition could place Canadian producers at a competitive disadvantage vis-avis foreign producers.
In his question of February 15, the hon. member called attention to the Halifax gateway study by A. O. Little. With respect to rail freight rates for containers the study indicates that those involving Halifax are quite reasonable relative to equivalent rates charged for container movement by rail in the U.S. Specifically, with respect to the existing container rate from Halifax to Chicago of $510 as opposed to $359 from Montreal to Chicago, this difference is reasonable when the distances for the two movements, 1,600 miles as compared to 800 miles, are considered. Mr. Speaker, rates reflect both distance and the cost of providing the service.
The study findings foresee continued growth in port and related distribution activity for Halifax and are therefore positive in terms of a growing and expanding role for the port of Halifax. Toward this goal, Mr. Speaker, the government of Canada will continue to work with all concerned. I think the hon. member opposite will agree that federal moneys for the construction of $35.6 million container handling facilities at Fairview Cove, Halifax, is just one demonstration of the federal government's commitment to this goal.

subtopic: POST OFFICE-REMOVAL OF TELEPHONES FROM RURAL POST OFFICES
POST OFFICE-REMOVAL OF TELEPHONES FROM RURAL POST OFFICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just prior to April 14 I received a phone call from a constituent in Ashern, Manitoba. I was informed by that constituent that the local post office had just been advised that their telephone was to be removed. I could not believe my ears when I heard that the post office, as part of their restraint program, was going to start removing telephones from rural post offices in Manitoba. That is why on April 14, under Standing Order 43, I brought up a motion which I felt was an urgent and pressing matter asking the post office to stop any further removal of telephones from rural post offices, because the telephone in a rural post office is the lifeline of the community.
At that particular time I thought the Post Office Department may have had the courtesy to advise me that telephones were to be removed from rural post offices in Manitoba. I was anxious to know if this procedure would be done Canada-wide or if it would be strictly confined to the province of Manitoba. I am glad to see the Postmaster General (Mr. Lamontagne) in the House tonight so he can answer this important question. To the rural people of Manitoba and maybe to people right across Canada I think this is certainly a sign that this government does not have much respect for the rural people and for the service which the post office should give them.
May 8, 1978

On May 4, the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) asked the Postmaster General why the post office was going back some 100 years to the Thomas Edison and Alexander Graham Bell era. The Postmaster General replied:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to answer this question but it seems quite irrelevant to me since the telephone does not come under the jurisdiction of the Post Office.
I learned something. I thought that would be under the jurisdiction of the post office. I was wondering if the Postmaster General had actually issued the order to remove the telephones.
Just what does the telephone mean to the local community? Let us take a typical rural community in my constituency in Manitoba. The postmaster knows everyone in that area. When someone's seed order, a COD parcel, eyeglasses that have been repaired or senior citizen's parcel arrives, it it only courtesy for the postmaster to telephone and inform that person. In many cases rural people live ten or 15 miles from the post office. The government says we must conserve energy. With the telephone removed from the post office, a person must drive to town to find out if a parcel has arrived. The post office is there to provide a service. When a parcel shipped by bus arrives in a rural community, the manager of the bus depot calls the person to tell him the parcel has arrived. If a parcel arrives by rail, the railway office makes a similar call. I feel we have gone back 100 years in this regard.
About 12 years ago in Manitoba, telephones were installed in grade five and grade four post office so that they could supervise the operations of some five or six smaller post offices in that region. Grade four post offices were generally in the immediate area of a grade five. The grade five postmaster was the supervisor of that area. He could make telephone calls regarding regulations and generally advise people of what was going on in the post office. It was toll free at that level.
The supervisoryship has been done away with. Some of the smaller post offices still telephone as a service regarding regulations and the availability of forms which post offices keep for the general public. Nowadays there is the steady telephone trade that has been created by the use of postal codes.
It appears that the decision to remove the telephones in Manitoba was made by one of the supervisors in Winnipeg. I understand his name is Mr. Gardner of the Winnipeg district office. While it may not be looked on as a cost-saving device, I understand it is a way of getting a little more money at the district level.
Most of the mail in the rural areas is now trucked from the major centres. There is always the chance that the truck driver may have trouble on the road, and he can call the postmaster and say that he will be four hours late. The postmaster will then not call in the extra help required for sorting mail.
I feel we have gone backward instead of forward. I would like to know exactly what security the Postmaster General is now giving the mail. The Queen's mail must have top priority as far as security is concerned.
Adjournment Debate
What will happen in the rural post office if there is a fire? What can the postmaster do? He cannot telephone the local fire department. That is why on May 4 I asked the Postmaster-General whether he had requisitioned hand bells. The postmaster could then run up and down the street, ringing his hand bell, shouting "Fire, fire". That is what was done before the telephone was invented.

subtopic: POST OFFICE-REMOVAL OF TELEPHONES FROM RURAL POST OFFICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question the hon. member has raised with respect to the control by Canada Post of telephones in rural post offices is certainly a surprising one. We are constantly beleaguered in this House by members across the aisle about post office deficits and alleged extravagance and incompetence in the operation of postal services. Yet when we move to rationalize an area in which taxpayers can save money, they complain.
The issue goes far beyond the line costs. These telephones were in use for many purposes which had nothing to do with the delivery of mail. Much of the time used on the phone and attending to the phone was related to personal rather than to post office business. So this is not just a financial but also a social issue and our policy with respect to it has been going on for many years without complaint. The great majority of rural post offices are situated in private homes or in small local businesses which have telephones of their own.
Again, we are faced with a question intended to dramatize the problem. What problem, Mr. Speaker? The hon. member has asked why we are now expecting people from outlying areas to drive into town to find out whether there is a parcel for them rather than telephone ahead to the post office before they leave their homes. Mr. Speaker, the population of Churchill riding-and I have great respect for them-know better. Citizens in urban areas are faced with the same problem, if indeed this is a problem. If a person living in a city is at work when our courier calls, the post office will deliver a notice that the parcel is at the post office. There is no need for the telephone. Our customers in rural areas are treated in the same manner. They, too, receive a notice that their parcel is at the post office where it can be picked up during regular hours. In the constituency of the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith), the communities of Church, Gillam, Lynn Lake, Leaf Rapids and Norway House still have phones and will continue to have phones if they wish. Our service concerns first class mail and we can efficiently maintain a good level of service by using first class mail.
The removal of the phone from some of these offices will not adversely affect the level of our service. If, for security or for some other good reason, a phone is needed, we at the post office are always open to consider such matters.
